newsitem.title: FRANCE: French digital television launch hits slight delay.
newsitem.headline: French digital television launch hits slight delay.

text.p: French television companies launched a new digital satellite television service with great fanfare on Monday night, although the service is not yet ready and nobody has a decoder at home to receive it.

"The sales campaign starts today and we can take subscriptions during the Christmas holiday, the decoders will be shipped in the second half of January," Patrick Le Lay, chairman of commercial broadcaster TF1 and TPS, told Le Figaro on Tuesday.
"At the end of 1997, TPS should have between 150,000 and 200,000 subscribers," he added.

Television par Satellite (TPS) is the much-hyped joint venture of commercial broadcasters TF1, M6 and Luxembourg's CLT, with cable operator Lyonnaise des Eaux and state-owned France Television and France Telecom. It had originally planned to start services before Christmas.

TPS aims to compete with Canal Plus's digital satellite offering, Canalsatellite, and smaller AB Sat, bringing the number of digital satellite broadcasters to three in France. Germany, Europe's biggest market, has one from Leo Kirch's group after Bertelsmann shelved its plans.
Canal Plus started its service in April and AB, whose parent company AB Productions was launched on the Nasdaq market last week, will start in the next few days.

TPS has a 12-channel offering at 90 francs ($17.25) per month, a movie service for 100 francs per month or a combined 150 franc per month subscription. A decoder can be bought for 3,000 francs or hired for 45 francs per month.
Canalsatellite subscriptions start at 98 francs per month.
TPS expects to make money with 700,000 subscribers which it hopes to have in the year 2000. Canalsatellite hopes to reach that point in 1998.

"The industry is developing very strongly and profitability is rising very fast. To give an indication, we expect Canalsatellite to reach breakeven during 1998," Canal Plus finance director Laurent Perpere told a magazine.
For Le Lay, who has been busy in the past few months lining up deals with Hollywood studios to offer movies, the difference between normal and satellite broadcasting lies in the cost.

"To broadcast their programmes all over France, the big four channels use a system of transmitters that cost about 500 million francs per year. If all households had digital satellite dishes, they would spend no more than five million," he said.
Guy de Panafieu, deputy executive chairman at Lyonnaise des Eaux, said the competition with Canalsatellite would be mainly on price.

"TPS aims to have the lowest price on the market. If you add the subscription prices of Canal Plus and Canalsatellite, you arrive at some 300 francs per month. That's very expensive when you look at the international market norm of digital television which is for $30 (150 francs) per month for 60 channels," he told La Tribune in an interview.
From February, Lyonnaise des Eaux will offer to swap analogue decoders at its cable subscribers with digital decoders.

While technical discussions are under way on the possibility of providing one decoder for all digital services -- a move the French government is actively promoting -- households will need at least two for the time being, one for Canal Plus and AB Sat and one for TPS.
-- Marcel Michelson, Paris newsroom +33 1 4221 5452 ($ = 5.216 French Francs)
